L000033	\begin{abstract}
L000034	We study the sedimentation of finite-size inertial particles in a
L000035	Rayleigh-Taylor-like setup using state-of-the-art direct numerical simulations.
L000036	The falling particles are observed to produce two distinct regions: a leading mixing layer with a linear concentration profile followed by a bulk region of uniform density.
L000037	Unlike classical RT turbulence, the mixing layer extension accelerates with an anomalous, non-integer exponent, while the bulk region moves at a constant velocity.
L000038	A one-dimensional model based on a local hindered settling law accurately captures the observed
L000039	dynamics and its dependence on the particle-to-fluid density ratio. The present work
L000040	identifies a new regime of convective mixing
L000041	which develops at the front of particle suspensions in sedimentation processes.

L000060	
L000061	
L000062	{\it Introduction.}
L000063	The problem of sedimentation has a long, rich history \cite{newton1687principia},
L000064	and its role in governing the natural world and shaping technical undertakings is well recognized \cite{lamb2020mud,koyaguchi1990sedimentation,meiburg-kneller2010,guazzelli2011physical}. Despite the deep-seated interest, however, the settling of particle collections remains an unsolved, formidable scientific challenge due to the dissipative nature of the fluid, the complex multi-body interactions and the emergence of a wide range of scales.
L000065	
L000066	Among the most immediate, and yet still open, questions
L000067	
L000068	is that of finding the average settling velocity $v$ of a suspension of solid particles. In fact, as particles settle, volume conservation produces an average upstream fluid motion.
L000069	This flow and its effects can be locally complex, and the overall sedimentation, when compared to the settling speed $v_t$ of a single particle, may be either hindered \cite{richardson1954sedimentation,batchelor1972,guazzelli2011physical} or enhanced \cite{huisman2016columnar}. For a suspension of solid fraction $\phi$, this problem is often referred to as that of finding the hindered settling function $f(\phi)=v/v_t$.
L000070	
L000071	
L000072	
L000073	
L000074	
L000075	
L000076	
L000077	
L000078	
L000079	
L000080	The initial distribution of the suspended particles (i.e. large scale spatial changes of $\phi$) can also affect the settling function.
L000081	One particularly relevant setup is that of a particle-laden suspension which sits atop the same clear, unladen fluid.
L000082	This condition
L000083	
L000084	is realized in a variety of natural
L000085	scenarios \cite{remington-arnett-ea1999,michioka2005instability,green1995plankton} and it is
L000086	relevant in the context of riverine outflows, where a sediment rich river can
L000087	form a hypopycnal flow, i.e. a superficial layer of dispersed sediment overlaid
L000088	on a body of water \cite{wells-dorrell2021,parsons-bush-ea2001}. The unstable
L000089	particle-laden layer collapses, forming plumes of particles which feed
L000090	convective shear layers and eventually turbulence.
L000091	In spite of the conceptual and practical relevance of the problem, fundamental
L000092	aspects remain scarcely investigated, with only few experimental
L000093	\cite{voltz-pesch-ea2001}, theoretical \cite{burns-meiburg2012} or numerical
L000094	\cite{chou-wu-ea2014,burns-meiburg2015,yu-hsu-ea2014,magnani-musacchio-ea2021}
L000095	works available mostly in the small inertia, high-dilution regime, where hindered settling effects are comparatively negligible.
L000096	
L000097	In this Letter, we investigate the yet unexplored regime of finite Stokes, finite dilution in the particle-laden Rayleigh-Taylor configuration, focusing our attention on the role of inertia.
L000098	
L000099	We use state-of-the-art, high-resolution direct numerical simulations to study the flow produced by the gravitational settling of $O(10^5)$ finite-size heavy particles layered above an otherwise quiescent fluid.
L000100	
L000101	
L000102	We observe the formation of a turbulent mixing layer in the advancing interfacial
L000103	region with a quasi-linear vertical profile of particle concentration, followed
L000104	by a bulk region in which particle density remains constant in time.
L000105	
L000106	
L000107	
L000108	At variance with the classical RT phenomenology \cite{boffetta2017incompressible},
L000109	we find that the evolution of the extension of the mixing layer
L000110	displays a power-law growth with an anomalous, non-integer exponent.
L000111	We develop a simple one-dimensional model of the hindered settling function
L000112	based on known physical ingredients, which is able to capture the
L000113	main features of the
L000114	turbulent
L000115	sedimentation process.
L000116	
L000117	
L000118	
L000119	{\it Model and observables.}
L000120	We consider a large number $\ndp$ of monodisperse spherical particles settling in a still fluid in the presence of gravity ${\bf g}=(0,0,-g)$.
L000121	Particles have diameter $d_p$ and density $\rho_p$ larger than that of the fluid $\rho_f$. The density ratio is $\gamma=\rho_p/\rho_f$.
L000122	
L000123	
L000124	At time $t=0$ the particles are randomly distributed exclusively in the top half of the domain, with an
L000125	initial particle volume fraction of $\phi_b$.
L000126	
L000127	The fluid phase is governed by the Navier-Stokes equations
L000128	\begin{equation}
L000129	{\partial {\bf u} \over \partial t} + {\bf u} \cdot {\bf \nabla u} =
L000130	{1 \over \rho_f} {\bf \nabla} p + \nu \nabla^2 {\bf u} + \frac{{\bf f}^{pf}}{\rho_f},
L000131	\label{eq1}
L000132	\end{equation}
L000133	for the incompressible velocity field ${\bf u}({\bf x},t)$.
L000134	${\bf f}^{pf}$ represents the coupling with the particles, whose motion is given by the Newton-Euler equations of motion for rigid spheres
L000135	\begin{equation}
L000136	m_p {d {\bm v}_p \over d t}={\bf f}_g+{\bf f}^{fp}+{\bf f}^{pp},
L000137	\label{eq2}
L000138	\end{equation}
L000139	\begin{equation}
L000140	I_p {d {\bf \omega}_p \over d t}={\bf L}^{fp}.
L000141	\label{eq3}
L000142	\end{equation}
L000143	Here, $m_p=\rho_p V_p$ is the mass of the particle of volume $V_p$, $I_p=m_p
L000144	d_p^2/10$ its moment of inertia, ${\bm v}_p$ and ${\bf \omega}_p$ are the
L000145	particle's translational and rotational velocities,
L000146	${\bf f}_g=(\gamma-1)\rho_f V_p {\bf g}$ the buoyancy force,
L000147	${\bf f}^{fp}$ and ${\bf L}^{fp}$ are
L000148	respectively the force and torque due to the fluid-particle interaction,
L000149	obtained as the particle surface integrals of the coupling force density
L000150	${\bf f}^{pf}$ and its moment with respect to the particle center
L000151	${\bf r_p}\times {\bf f}^{pf}$.
L000152	
L000153	Direct numerical simulations of the equations (\ref{eq1}--\ref{eq3}) are performed using the in-house developed finite-difference solver \emph{Fujin} (see Supplemental Material~\cite{supp}). The equations are discretised in a vertically elongated domain of size $L_x\times L_y\times L_z$, where $L_x=L_y$ and $L_z=4L_x$.
L000154	Periodic boundary conditions are imposed on the horizontal directions $(x,y)$, while no-slip, no-penetration conditions are set on the top and bottom of the domain.
L000155	Following the system's symmetries, the collective dynamics of the particle ensemble can be described in terms of the vertical profiles of the local volume fraction $\phi(z,t)$ and of the
L000156	particle vertical velocity $v(z,t)$, averaged over the horizontal planes. The initial condition for our setup then corresponds to $\phi(z,0) = 0$ for $0 < z < L_z/2$ and $\phi(z,0) = \phi_b$ for $L_z/2 < z < L_z$, while $v(z,0)=0$ in all the domain. We set $\ndp=10^5$ corresponding to $\phi_b\approx0.10$.
L000157	We investigate four different values of the particle-to-fluid density ratio $\gamma={2,4,8,16}$.
L000158	In order to develop a mathematical model for the mixing layer, we performed additional simulations at volume fractions $\phi_b=0.05$ and $\phi_b=0.15$.
L000159	
L000160	
L000161	
L000162	Figure~\ref{fig1} shows a snapshot of the system partway through its evolution for the $\gamma=2$ case.
L000163	At time $t=0$ particles begin to fall from the upper part of the domain. The motion is however not uniform, and the formation of plume-like structures in the suspension causes particles closer to the interface with free fluid to fall faster. This produces a complex interfacial region in which the fluid becomes turbulent and affects the dynamics of the falling particles.
L000164	
L000165	
L000166	\begin{figure}[h!]
L000167	\centerline{\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{t27.pdf}}
L000168	\caption{Volumetric rendering of the instantaneous vertical fluid velocity
L000169	field $v_z({\bm x},t)$ and particle positions at $t\approx0.17\tau_t$.
L000170	Upward/downward velocities are shown in blue/orange, more intense
L000171	for higher magnitudes of $v_z$. Regions where $v_z\approx0$ are rendered as
L000172	transparent.}
L000173	\label{fig1}
L000174	\end{figure}
L000175	
L000176	
L000177	
L000178	
L000179	
L000180	
L000181	
L000182	
L000183	
L000184	Figure~\ref{fig2} displays the vertical profile of particle concentration
L000185	$\phi(z,t)$ for the case $\gamma=2$ at different times.
L000186	In spite of the complexity of the dynamics, vertical profile has a relatively simple form with two distinct regions.
L000187	In the upper part $z_1(t) \le z \le z_2(t)$ (the ``bulk'') the volume fraction
L000188	remains uniform and equal to the original value $\phi_b$,
L000189	while in the lower part
L000190	$z_0(t) \le z \le z_1(t)$ (the ``mixing region'') the particle-laden phase mixes with the unladen
L000191	fluid, resulting in a non-uniform concentration developing a close to linear
L000192	profile. Both the bulk and the mixing regions fall but with
L000193	different velocities, and therefore the shape of the profile changes in time.
L000194	Based on these observations, we model the concentration profile with a simple
L000195	piecewise linear function
L000196	\begin{equation}
L000197	\phi(z,t) = \left\{
L000198	\begin{array}{ll}
L000199	 0 & z \le z_0 \land z > z_2 \\
L000200	\phi_b \frac{z-z_0}{z_1-z_0} & z_0 \le z \le z_1 \\
L000201	\phi_b & z_1 \le z \le z_2
L000202	\end{array}
L000203	\right.
L000204	\label{eq4}
L000205	\end{equation}
L000206	From the points in (\ref{eq4}), we define the extension of the mixing
L000207	region $h(t)=z_1-z_0$ and its central point
L000208	$z_c(t)=(z_1+z_0)/2$. Volume conservation requires that the distance
L000209	$z_2-z_c$ remains constant.
L000210	
L000211	
L000212	\begin{figure}
L000213	\centerline{\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{statsibmgamma2-eps-converted-to.pdf}}
L000214	\caption{Particle concentration profiles for the $\gamma=2$ case at different
L000215	times. Dashed lines represent the profile model (\ref{eq4}) together with the positions of its characteristic points $z_0$, $z_1$ and $z_2$ for the latest time. In the inset, the latest three curves are rescaled according to the instantaneous locations of $z_0$ and $z_1$.}
L000216	\label{fig2}
L000217	\end{figure}
L000218	
L000219	
L000220	
L000221	Figure~\ref{fig3} displays the time evolution of the width $h(t)$ and of the center $z_c(t)$
L000222	of the mixing region for the four cases at different density ratio.
L000223	For each run, the values of $z_0(t)$, $z_1(t)$ and $z_2(t)$ are obtained by a fit of the numerical data with the piecewise linear function (\ref{eq4}) at the different times.
L000224	Figure~\ref{fig3} shows that while $z_c(t)$ (and therefore $z_2$) moves approximately
L000225	with a constant velocity $v_b$, proportional to the terminal velocity of a single particle $v_t$,
L000226	the growth of $h(t)$ is accelerated with respect to $v_t$. This effect is strongly dependent on the density ratio, and becomes more important for smaller values of $\gamma$.
L000227	
L000228	The different velocities observed in the bulk and mixing regions
L000229	arise from differences in the suspension local structure.
L000230	
L000231	In the bulk of the suspension, where particles remain homogeneously
L000232	distributed, the particle falling speed is reduced with respect to a single
L000233	particle because of the change in background flow speed due to the fluid rising
L000234	homogeneously through the bulk.
L000235	By comparing the simulations at different volume fractions, we find that,
L000236	this reduced hindered settling velocity is proportional to $\phi_b$, i.e.
L000237	$v_b \simeq v_t(a- d \phi_b)$ (where $a$ and $d$ are constants of order one independent
L000238	on $\gamma$, see Supplementary material), within the range of parameters explored.
L000239	This is reminescent of the Richardson-Zaki (RZ) relation for the hindered
L000240	settling velocity of Stokesian inertial particles which is valid for
L000241	small particle Reynolds number $Re_p$ \cite{richardson1954sedimentation}.
L000242	
L000243	
L000244	
L000245	
L000246	
L000247	
L000248	
L000249	
L000250	
L000251	
L000252	
L000253	
L000254	Inside the mixing region, the particle velocity is not constant, as particles segregate into falling plumes (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}), and, as a result, are accelerated by wake effects. This is reflected in the $z$-dependence of the local volume fraction $\phi$.
L000255	
L000256	
L000257	To account for these physical ingredients, we propose a simple 1D model for the
L000258	evolution of the relative concentration based on mass conservation and its
L000259	transport by the vertical velocity
L000260	\begin{equation}
L000261	{\partial \phi \over \partial t}=-{\partial \over \partial z}
L000262	\left( v \phi \right),
L000263	\label{eq5}
L000264	\end{equation}
L000265	where $v$ is given by a
L000266	local hindered model which generalizes the result observed
L000267	for the bulk region
L000268	\begin{equation}
L000269	v(z,t) =  - v_0 \left( 1 - c \phi(z,t) \right),
L000270	\label{eq6}
L000271	\end{equation}
L000272	where $v_0$ is the velocity of the front position $x_0$
L000273	and $c=(v_0-v_b)/(v_0 \phi_b)$ represents
L000274	the relative velocity difference between the front and the bulk of
L000275	particle distribution.
L000276	
L000277	
L000278	\begin{figure}[h]
L000279	
L000280	\centerline{\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{mixwidth_sep-eps-converted-to.pdf}}
L000281	\caption{Time evolution of the width $h(t)$ (filled symbols) and geometric center $z_c(t)$ (empty symbols) of the mixing region for the simulations at different
L000282	$\gamma$. For the geometric center, a black continuous line of slope $r$ is included for guidance.
L000283	}
L000284	\label{fig3}
L000285	\end{figure}
L000286	
L000287	
L000288	Assuming, as
L000289	shown by the inset of Fig.~\ref{fig2}, that the concentration profile inside the mixing region is a self-similar function $\phi(z,t) = \phi_b f(\tilde{z})$ of the non-dimensional variable $\tilde{z} = (z-z_c(t))/h(t)$,  we obtain from (\ref{eq5}--\ref{eq6}) the relation
L000290	\begin{equation}
L000291	\tilde{z} {dh \over dt} + {dz_c \over dt} =
L000292	- \left[ v_0 + 2 (v_b-v_0) f(\tilde{z}) \right],
L000293	\label{eq7}
L000294	\end{equation}
L000295	which shows that $f(\tilde{z})$ must be the linear function
L000296	$f(\tilde{z}) = 1/2 + \tilde{z}$ in the mixing region
L000297	$|\tilde{z}| \le 1/2$, which indeed corresponds to the profile (\ref{eq4}).
L000298	
L000299	The center of the mixing region moves downward at the same speed of the bulk
L000300	$v_b$, while the growth of the mixing region is determined by the difference
L000301	between the velocity of the front $v_0$ and of the bulk $v_b$:
L000302	\begin{equation}
L000303	\frac{d z_c}{dt} = -v_b \;, \;\;   \frac{d h}{dt} = 2 (v_0-v_b)
L000304	\label{eq8}
L000305	\end{equation}
L000306	
L000307	The velocity difference $v_0-v_b$ is due to the turbulent motions inside the
L000308	mixing region, the intensity of which depends in general on $h$ and on the density
L000309	ratio $\gamma$. By factorizing this dependence as
L000310	$v_0-v_b \propto v_b (\gamma-1)^\beta (h/L_z)^\alpha$, and using the
L000311	fact that $v_b=r v_t$, we finally obtain the predictions:
L000312	\begin{equation}
L000313	\frac{z_c(t)-z_c(0)}{L_z} = -r \frac{t}{\tau_t} \;, \;\;
L000314	\frac{h(t)}{L_z} = b \left(\frac{t}{\tau_t}(\gamma-1)^\beta\right)^\xi ,
L000315	\label{eq9}
L000316	\end{equation}
L000317	where we have introduced the settling time of a single particle
L000318	$\tau_t = L_z/v_t$, $\xi = 1/(1-\alpha)$, and $\beta$ and the integration constant $b$ (which depends on the initial volume fraction) are fitting parameters.
L000319	
L000320	
L000321	
L000322	\begin{figure}[h]
L000323	
L000324	\centerline{\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{mixwidth-eps-converted-to.pdf}}
L000325	\caption{Time evolution of the width $h(t)$ of the mixing region.
L000326	Results from different $\gamma$ are rescaled according to the model (\ref{eq9}),
L000327	which is represented by the black continuous line.
L000328	}
L000329	\label{fig4}

L000342	We fit the time evolution of $h(t)$ shown in Fig.~\ref{fig3}
L000343	with the prediction (\ref{eq9}).
L000344	Remarkably, we find the values of the exponent $\xi$ to be independent of $\gamma$, and we compute its average value and the error as $\xi=1.375 \pm 0.015$.
L000345	We find that all the runs are very well fitted with
L000346	$\beta=-1/3$, which is therefore fixed, and the coefficient $b$ is
L000347	obtained as $b = 3.75 \pm 0.10$. Incidentally, we note that the sustained acceleration of the mixing layer expansion ($\xi>1$) effectively translates into settling enhancement at late times, with $v_0$ growing up to $1.5v_t$ for case $\gamma=2$ within the investigated time span.

L000349	
L000350	In Fig.~\ref{fig4} we plot the mixing layer width $h(t)$ rescaled according
L000351	to the model using the above parameters
L000352	together with the analytic prediction (\ref{eq9}).
L000353	The remarkable quality of the rescaling indicates that our 1D model is indeed
L000354	able to capture the complex dynamics of the evolution of particle distribution in a
L000355	wide range of density ratio.
L000356	The fact that the exponent $\beta$ of the density ratio $\gamma$ is
L000357	negative reflects quantitatively what observed in Fig.~\ref{fig3},
L000358	i.e., that the mixing layer is more accelerated with respect to the
L000359	single particle velocity $v_t$ for lower density ratio.
L000360	
L000361	Of course, this behavior cannot be extended to
L000362	very small values of $\gamma-1$, because of the divergence of
L000363	(\ref{eq9}) as $\gamma \to 1$. Nonetheless, in the wide range of
L000364	density ratio investigated by our simulations, the scaling exponent
L000365	$\beta=-1/3$ is able to describe the observed phenomenology.
L000366	
L000367	The hindered model (\ref{eq5}--\ref{eq6}) allows us to make quantitative predictions for
L000368	
L000369	other important quantities, such as the particle flux. This is defined as
L000370	\begin{equation}
L000371	\Pi(z,t)=-v(z,t) \phi(z,t),
L000372	\label{eq10}
L000373	\end{equation}
L000374	and represents the vertical flux of the solid phase. A reference value for this flux is that corresponding to a rigid motion of the bulk of particles with velocity $v_b$, that is $\Pi_b=v_b \phi_b$. The model prediction for the particle flux in the mixing region $|\tilde{z}|\le 1/2$ has the simple expression in the non-dimensional variable $\tilde{z}$
L000375	\begin{equation}
L000376	{\Pi(z,t) \over \Pi_b} = \left({1 \over 2}+\tilde{z} \right)+{v_0-v_b \over v_b} \left({1 \over 4}-\tilde{z}^2 \right),
L000377	\label{eq11}
L000378	\end{equation}
L000379	where we remark that both $\tilde{z}$ and $v_0$ are functions of time.

L000389	Figure~\ref{fig5} shows that the prediction (\ref{eq11}) reproduces well the numerical vertical flux obtained from our simulations. We remark that no additional parameter is fitted in (\ref{eq11}) since all the coefficients are fixed from the time evolution of $h(t)$.
L000390	A distinctive feature of the particle flux is the presence of a maximum just below the bulk region. This is due to particles accelerated from the lower boundary of the bulk region by the turbulent-like flow in the mixing region and is well captured by the model prediction (\ref{eq11}).

L000397	{\it Conclusions.}
L000398	We studied the dynamics of a layer of finite-size heavy particles
L000399	sedimenting in an initially quiescent fluid. In spite of the
L000400	complexity of the phenomenon, which produces a non-homogeneous
L000401	turbulent-like flow, we find that,
L000402	in the parameter space explored,
L000403	the particle concentration profile
L000404	follows a self-similar evolution with a linear mixing layer
L000405	followed by a bulk region of constant concentration.
L000406	Due to differences in the local structure of the suspension among the two regions, we observe both hindrance and enhancement of the average particle settling speeds.
L000407	
L000408	Compared to the classic Rayleigh-Taylor phenomenology, which predicts quadratic scaling for $h(t)$, we find a superlinear but less-than-quadratic power law growth of the mixing layer, with scaling exponent  $\xi\approx1.37$
L000409	in the range of parameters investigated.
L000410	
L000411	To elucidate the effect of the observed dynamics, we introduce a one-dimensional transport model based on the observation of a RZ-like hindered settling relation within the bulk region, and its further local extension within the mixing layer, which we find justified \emph{a posteriori}.
L000412	The model is able to explain both the anomalous scaling and its dependence on the density ratio, and is able to accurately predict quantities such as the vertical particle flux.
L000413	Note that, the standard RT phenomenology is expected in the limit $d_p \to 0$ and $n_p \propto d_p^{-3}$, such that the dynamics of the particles recovers that of Lagrangian tracers and the density difference
L000414	between the suspension and the pure fluid remains finite.
L000415	This regime is outside the parameter space explored here.
L000416	
L000417	
L000418	
L000419	
L000420	
L000421	This work represents only a first step in understanding the dynamics of inertial suspensions at large concentrations. Future works will be required to better characterize the fundamental mechanics driving the anomalous mixing layer expansion. Moreover, there would be additional value in further extending our investigation to other regions of the parameter space, as well as comparing with the results of laboratory experiments.

L000875	\section{Domain and resolution}
L000876	For the cases presented in the main text, equations (1--3) are solved in a vertically elongated domain of size $L_x\times L_y\times L_z$, where $L_x=L_y=2\pi$ and $L_z=4L_x$. On the basis of the chosen spatial resolution, this corresponds to $384 \times 384 \times 1536$ collocation points.
L000877	
L000878	Statistical convergence was improved through repeated realizations of the flow, and the results averaged. In particular, for each case of particle inertia investigated, three independent realizations of the flow were performed, differing in the initial uniformly random distribution of particles in the top half of the domain.
L000879	For the purpose of the quantities investigated in this work, the cross-realization variance has been found to be sufficiently small as to be negligible.

L000997	\section{Numerical method}
L000998	
L000999	The simulations presented in the work are performed using \emph{Fujin}, a in-house finite-difference incompressible fluid solver which features a second-order central finite difference scheme in space and second order Adams-Bashforth in time. The incompressibility constraint is enforced through a fractional step method.
L001000	
L001001	Fluid-particle coupling is obtained through the use of the Eulerian Immersed Boundary Method (IBM) developed by \citet{hori-rosti-ea2022}. The particle position is tracked as a single Lagrangian point, while its footprint on the color function is discretized directly on the fluid simulation grid through the use of a fast hyperbolic tangent digitizer. The method includes implicit lubrication and an additional soft particle collision model. It has been extensively validated (\url{https://www.oist.jp/research/research-units/cffu/validation}) and used in previous works on particle-laden flows \citep{chiarini-cannon-ea2024,chiarini-tandurella-ea2025}.
L001002	Despite the presence of a collisional contacts model, we find that, in the range of parameters investigated in this Letter, collisions do not play any meaningful role; indeed, at volume fraction $10\,\%$ and $\gamma=2$ we observe that only a fraction of particles smaller than $0.001$ is in contact at any instant. This fraction grows at most to $\approx0.018$ for $\gamma=16$.
L001003	
L001004	
L001005	
L001006	
L001007	\section{Fitting the concentration profiles}
L001008	
L001009	The vertical profile of the volume fraction $\phi(z,t)$ is defined as $\phi(z,t)\equiv\langle \Phi({\bm x},t) \rangle_{xy}$, where $\Phi({\bm x},t)$ is the particle field color function (equal to 1 inside the particles and 0 outside), and $\langle \cdot \rangle_{xy}$ represents the average over the horizontal planes of the domain. A similar definition is used for the particle vertical velocity $v(z,t) \equiv \langle \Phi({\bm x},t) v_z({\bm x},t)\rangle_{xy} / \phi(z,t)$.
L001010	
L001011	The numerical concentration profiles $\phi(z,t)$ are fitted, for each time, by the piecewise linear function
L001012	\begin{equation}
L001013	\phi(z,t) = \left\{
L001014	\begin{array}{ll}
L001015	 0 & z \le z_0 \land z > z_2 \\
L001016	\phi_b \frac{z-z_0}{z_1-z_0} & z_0 \le z \le z_1 \\
L001017	\phi_b & z_1 \le z \le z_2 \\
L001018	\end{array}
L001019	\right.
L001020	\label{eq1}
L001021	\end{equation}
L001022	with all the parameters $\phi_b(t)$ and $z_i(t)$ free at each time.
L001023	
L001024	We find that value of $\phi_b\approx 0.103$ to be independent on time, showing no compaction nor expansion of the bulk during the evolution of the system.
L001025	
L001026	
L001027	Due to the discrete nature of the particles, the measured spatial profiles of volume fraction and velocity present small scale noise. In order to correctly represent the salient features of the data, we smooth out the small scale noise through a coarse-graining procedure.
L001028	In particular, we apply a fixed \num{33} grid-point (corresponding to $\num{0.02}L_z$ or $\num{5.5}\ddp$) rolling average stencil to the measured $\phi(z,t)$ and $\Pi(z,t)$ presented respectively in Fig.~2 and Fig.~5 of the main text.
L001029	We remark that this coarse-graining procedure is performed only for display purposes, while the raw data is used for the fitting procedure.
